claims.text: The additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy has a single-phase FCC matrix.
The starting alloy has high strength and fatigue performance.
The starting alloy is chemically homogeneous and has minimal pre-existing oxide coverage.
Elevated-temperature degradation of this alloy is governed by selective oxidation of Al and Ti.
Al and Ti diffuse to the surface and along grain boundaries during elevated-temperature exposure.
Selective oxidation produces a heterogeneous scale composed primarily of Al2O3 and TiO2.
Cr-containing oxides may also contribute to the scale.
The external oxide scale initially acts as a protective barrier.
Thermal-expansion mismatch and oxide brittleness generate stresses that eventually cause scale spallation and microcracking.
Under reducing conditions, incomplete external oxidation produces internal oxidation localized at high-diffusivity paths.
Oxide spallation, microcracking, and internal oxidation reduce local mechanical integrity and degrade fatigue life, strength, or hardness.
The proposed degradation can occur without gross phase transformation of the FCC matrix.
Oxidizing exposure will produce a more extensive external oxide scale than reducing exposure.
Continued oxidizing exposure will increase oxide-scale spallation and localized microcrack formation relative to the as-manufactured baseline.
Reducing-atmosphere samples will exhibit less surface oxide but may exhibit more internal oxidation than oxidizing-atmosphere samples.
The proposed degradation mechanism becomes significant above approximately 800 °C after more than 100 hours of exposure.
Below approximately 800 °C or 100 hours, oxidation and internal degradation will be minimal.
A lack of atmosphere-dependent oxide morphology and mechanical-property changes, or degradation without selective oxidation or spallation, would falsify the proposed mechanism.
